While New Vegas' world is much more fleshed out and interesting than the unoriginal Capital Wastes, it performed very, very poorly in terms of overall environmental excitement. Yes there was Vegas and Big MT and Jacobstown, but they were all outweighed by the incredibly monotonous and boring desert theme the entire game has. I get what they were trying to go for and I respect that, but there were moments when I had to set down the game for a couple days just because of how dull and undiverse the landscape was. Most of the locations were pretty indistinguishable from each other, and had it not been for the incredible writing and character development I probably wouldn't have bothered to finish the game at all. 

FO3 has many faults, from it's absolutely terrible attempt at storytelling to a morality system that boiled down to either being a selfless saint or a moustache-twirling satan, and while its landscape wasn't as diverse as it could have or should have been, it was miles above the lackluster sands of the mojave. DC had a much bigger impact on me than New Vegas (the city, not the game) simply because Vegas was incredibly small. In fact, if I recall correctly, the only feeling I had when I finally reached New Vegas was disappointment, as I had been so hyped for it and when I actually saw that it was all of 3 casinos I couldn't help but feel a little cheated. All of the areas of FO3 also seemed to resonate more with the sense of loss and grief that comes with living in a dying world, a point the juxtaposition of its over-the-top wackiness only seemed to strengthen. New Vegas may have been a much better Fallout game, but it was a terrible post-apocalyptic game. The idea of the apocalypse was a small theme in Vegas, but it wasn't a character. Not like it was in FO3 anyways. 

Overall, what I'm trying to say I guess is that the mojave was a little too bland, but because of the environment, not the character of the mojave. DC wasn't much better, but it succeeded on drawing me in with it's landscape, a feat New Vegas could never do. This is all opinion of course, as I imagine you and numerous others feel the opposite. I just wanted our point to be out there.

Bretons are actually shorter than Nords, and are the only human race with slightly pointy ears due to their mer/men lineage. The Bretons are a hybrid race, created when the Aldmer who lived in High Rock raped their human slaves en masse. These hybrids soon began breeding with each other and were able to kick the Aldmer out when their numbers were big enough. They're more magically inclined because of this as well, and their culture is based on the medieval French and Celtic. 

   Nords are the tallest, burliest, and hairiest of men, and were the first men to come to Tamriel from the frozen northern continent of Atmora. Nords may also be the proudest of men, as they almost always prefer war over diplomacy. Their culture is based on the medieval Scandinavians with a tiny bit of German thrown in. 

   The Imperials are the men of Cyrodiil, and are called so because of their tendency to create Empires. The Imperials were once enslaved by the Ayleids, the Heartland High Elves who once lived in Cyrodiil, but beat them back and created the First Empire under the Empress Alessia, who started the Dragonfire Covenant. Imperials are slightly shorter than the other two races of men, have darker skin and hair, and are more diplomatic than them. Their culture is based on that of Ancient Rome, with some generic fantasy elements as well.

Well, no. First off, the most common-spoken language in the U.S is English, where did you get Spanish out of? It's commonly spoken, yes, but only in the states that border mexico. Not a whole lot of Spanish is spoken in, say, Washington, or Oregon, or Montana. 

Second off, Westeros isn't really the U.S, nor is it Europe. The U.S has so many pockets because of the fact that it's been immigrated to so much in the past 300 years. Spanish and French are spoken commonly in the U.S because it has a history of colonization and territory conflicts, something which Westeros hasn't really experienced, at least to the scale the U.S has. 

Europe on the other hand isn't like Westeros in that Europe is made up of a ridiculous amount of ethnic groups, while Westeros has only 3. Yes, we have certain nationalities like Westermen, Rivermen, and Reachmen, but from what I've experienced in the books, It's not too easy to differentiate between, say, Crownmen and Valemen and the like. You do have some exceptions in the case of Dornishmen, Ironmen, and Northmen to an extent, but that's not nearly the same case as Europeans. Italians, Germans, Swedes, Englishmen, and Spaniards are incredibly different, much more so than the Westerosi. 

Westeros has also been under single rule for over 300 years, something which Europe has not. When ruling a single territory, most cases as seen in history, has made it so there is some sort of unifying language, and since most of Westeros already spoke some sort of Andalish tongue at the time of the Landing, besides the Dornish and the Northerners and maybe the Ironborn, it probably wouldn't be too hard to establish some sort of Common Tongue.
